subject: mathematics
question_text: Find the volume of the tetrahedron whose vertices are (1,2,1), (3,2,5), (2,−1,0) and (−1,0,1).

mark_split.label: Find the three edge vectors from A
Divide by 6 and state the volume

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Junior Inter Maths-1A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.64 — SAQ chapter 9 Product of Vectors, answer 61. Printed appearances: TS 15,20. The difference from answer 60 is that VERTICES are given, not edges — so three subtractions come first. The book notes "Tetra means 4", which is the count of vertices, not of edges.THE MARK SPLIT IS PRINTED in that book's margin as [1 Mark] on the edge vectors, [2 Marks] on the determinant and [1 Mark] on the volume — a sourced 1+2+1 — a sourced split, not an inference. The book's chapter header carries ★★ and reads '4 Marks'; that star is the CHAPTER's rank, not this question's. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Paper position: Maths-1A Section B runs Q11-Q17 at 4 marks each, answer any 5 of 7; Q13 is the Product of Vectors slot. LINES EXPANDED 2026-09-14 (founder direction, modelled on the Maths-2A and Maths-2B expansions): every move is written on its own line, with the reason or the arithmetic shown before it is used; the steps, marks and split are unchanged.

recall_prompt: Say how you would find the volume of a tetrahedron from its four vertices.
formula_note: Volume of a tetrahedron is (1/6)|[a b c]| where a, b, c are three edges from one vertex — here the question gives four VERTICES, so AB, AC, AD must be formed first before the box product. A sibling question gives the edges directly; do not skip the subtraction step here.

steps.label: Find the three edges
steps.margin_note: First mark. Four vertices, but only THREE edges are needed — the simplest choice is all three from corner A. That is what turns vertices into the form the formula wants.
steps.memory_tip: Four vertices but only THREE edges are needed. Take all three from corner A.

steps.why: Three edges from one corner are the simplest choice. Three edges that lie in one face, such as AB, BC and CA, would give a flat box with no volume.
common_mistakes: Using three edges that lie in one face, such as AB, BC and CA, which gives 0.
Missing a zero component — AB has no j term and AD has no k term.

steps.why: A negative triple product just means the three edges are ordered the other way round. The modulus in the formula removes that, which is why a volume is still positive.
common_mistakes: Assuming the negative determinant is a mistake and re-doing correct arithmetic.
Forgetting the minus sign in front of the middle term of the expansion.

steps.label: Divide by 6
steps.margin_note: Last mark. The modulus turns −36 into 36, and a sixth of that is 6. Cubic units.
steps.memory_tip: The modulus turns −36 into 36, and a sixth of that is 6. Cubic units.

recall.must_convey: That the modulus of −36 divided by 6 gives a volume of 6 cubic units.
accept: mod of minus thirty six over six is six cubic units

steps.why: The modulus is doing real work here — without it the answer would be −6, which is not a volume.

insider_note: Vertices are given, not edges, so subtract first to get AB, AC and AD all starting at A. The modulus matters: −36 gives a volume of 6, never −6.
